analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 25% minimum tax on income plus unrealized gains for households worth over $100 million.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a floor vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require households with more than $100 million in net worth to pay a minimum tax of 25% each year on their regular income plus the increase in the paper value of assets they have not sold. Tax paid on gains that are only on paper is credited back when the assets are actually sold, so taxpayers are not taxed twice on the same gain. The bill also closes common ways wealthy families avoid the tax, including shifting assets into trusts or giving them away before death.
analysis.who_benefits: No spending purpose is written into the bill, so the direct beneficiary is the tax code itself: under current law, most of the income of very wealthy households comes from gains on assets that are never taxed until sold, and often never taxed at all if held until death. The bill would make roughly 0.01% of households pay closer to 25% on that income each year, and any revenue would flow to the general treasury, easing pressure on everyone else's taxes or on deficits.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes an annual minimum tax equal to 25% of a household's taxable income plus its net unrealized gains, for anyone whose net worth exceeds $100 million, capped so the tax cannot exceed 40% of net worth above $100 million.

Tax paid on unrealized gains is not a permanent extra tax: when a taxpayer actually sells assets and recognizes the gain, the minimum tax previously paid is credited against the tax on that gain, and any excess is refundable.

The bill counts assets moved into trusts and gifts or bequests made within a 5- to 10-year lookback window toward the taxpayer's net worth, and makes gifts, charitable contributions, and transfers at death taxable events for people who were subject to the tax, aimed at preventing avoidance.

Taxpayers holding illiquid assets such as stakes in private companies can elect to pay in 5 to 9 annual installments, and a special deferral regime lets them postpone payment on non-tradable assets until they are sold or transferred, with interest accruing.

analysis.who_pays: Households with net worth above $100 million — a few tens of thousands of taxpayers — who would owe tax annually on gains from unsold assets, including large stockholders and owners of private companies, trusts holding their assets, and estates of people who were covered within the prior 10 years.

drawbacks.text: Taxing unrealized gains requires valuing assets that are not publicly traded every year; the bill leaves most valuation methods to Treasury regulations, defaults to formula-based estimates for non-tradable assets absent guidance, and would add a substantial new net-worth and asset reporting regime.

For owners of private companies, the tax could force asset sales or borrowing to pay a bill on paper wealth; the bill addresses this with installment elections and a deferral regime with accruing interest, but that deferral itself carries a lifetime of administrative obligations and a retrospective reconciliation charge when the account resolves.

The bill also makes charitable contributions a taxable event for covered taxpayers (with regulation-defined exceptions), which would raise the cost of large charitable giving by the ultra-wealthy and could reduce large donations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design tries to answer the classic objections to taxing unrealized gains — double taxation is avoided through credits, liquidity through installments and deferral — but the cost is a large, regulation-heavy valuation and reporting apparatus whose accuracy depends on rules Treasury had not yet written. If enforced as designed, the burden falls almost entirely on the top sliver of households; the main practical risk is that valuation disputes and avoidance planning blunt the revenue it raises.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never scheduled it for a hearing or markup, and the 118th Congress ended with the bill still sitting there.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the Billionaire Minimum Income Tax Act on November 29, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation.
61 House members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats; no Republican cosponsored it.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with more than $100 million in net worth, particularly holders of large unrealized gains in stocks and private companies, are better off because the bill died: no annual minimum tax on unrealized gains was created, and the existing rules that defer tax on unsold assets until death remain in place. Wealth management and estate-planning structures that rely on those rules also remain untouched.

sides.party_line_note: All 61 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; Republicans controlled the House and the Ways and Means Committee, and no Republican supported the bill, so it went nowhere.

industries.industry: Households with more than $100 million in net worth
industries.note: The bill would tax gains on assets they have not sold, ending the current arrangement where large paper fortunes are untaxed year after year and often go untaxed at death. The interest of this group runs against the public's in the narrow sense that the tax they would pay is the revenue and tax-fairness gain for everyone else.

The bill taxes gifts and transfers at death by covered taxpayers and pulls trust-attributed assets and recent gratuitous transfers into the net-worth calculation, shrinking demand for the trust and gifting structures these firms sell to defer or avoid tax.
